questions.q: Name the system through which industrial workers were recruited in early 19th-century British factories and identify who controlled it.
questions.a: The jobber system: jobbers (often old trusted workers) recruited villagers, gave loans, and controlled entry. A wrong answer like "factory managers directly hired" reveals the student misses the intermediary role that bound workers through debt and loyalty.

questions.q: Explain why factory owners in seasonal industries (like gas works or breweries) preferred hand labour over machines even after steam power was available.
questions.a: Machines required high fixed capital and could not be idled cheaply; hand labour could be hired/fired seasonally. If a student says "machines were not invented yet", they confuse technological availability with economic rationality — a classic board exam trap.

questions.q: A cotton mill in 1840s Lancashire employs 200 women and 100 men for the same spinning task. Women are paid 6 shillings/week, men 10 shillings. Using the concept of 'reserve army of labour', explain why the mill owner maintains this gap.
questions.a: Women were seen as secondary earners; their lower reservation wage and social norms allowed owners to depress wages. A wrong answer citing "women were less skilled" ignores that many women had equal skill from domestic spinning — the gap was structural, not ability-based.

questions.q: Compare the living conditions of a migrant worker in a British industrial town (c. 1840) with a peasant artisan in pre-industrial India (c. 1750). Identify two similarities and two differences in their vulnerability to economic shocks.
questions.a: Similarities: both dependent on employers/merchants, both faced income uncertainty. Differences: the migrant worker faced urban overcrowding and factory discipline; the artisan faced rural indebtedness and loss of craft control. A student listing only "both were poor" fails to analyse structural causes — a common omission in case-based questions.

questions.q: Critique the statement: "The entry of women into factories during the Industrial Revolution was a step towards gender equality." Use evidence from wages, working conditions, and social attitudes.
questions.a: It was not equality but exploitation: women earned half of men's wages, worked in worse conditions, and were barred from skilled trades; middle-class reformers later pushed them out citing morality. A student agreeing with the statement confuses presence with empowerment — a frequent error in evaluation questions.

questions.q: Construct a 4-panel storyboard (described in words) showing the journey of a young woman from a Bengal village to a jute mill in Calcutta in the 1890s, highlighting the role of the jobber, the voyage, factory discipline, and her wage relative to male workers.
questions.a: Panel 1: Jobber advances money to family, recruits her. Panel 2: Steamer journey, crowded, supervised. Panel 3: Mill gate, strict timing, noise, 12-hour shift. Panel 4: Pay day — she receives 4 rupees, male coworker gets 7 for same task. A weak storyboard misses the jobber's power or the wage gap, showing incomplete grasp of gendered labour markets.
